title: Barmen (1934)
hook: Protestant Christians of the Confessing Church declare that Christ, not Hitler, is Lord
carry: jesus christ is the one word

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dorothy Day, a pot of soup, and the works of mercy treated as a job description.

Swastika flags hang inside some German churches. A movement calling itself the German Christians wants the Protestant church folded into the new state, a national bishop loyal to Hitler, and pastors of Jewish descent pushed out. Some pastors go along. Others don't. They gather in a church in Barmen, an industrial town on the Wupper river, Lutherans, Reformed and United side by side, and they write a short statement. It doesn't name Hitler once. It doesn't need to.

The group that met at Barmen came to be called the Confessing Church, because what they did was confess, in the old sense: say out loud what they believed. The theologian Karl Barth did much of the drafting. The declaration follows a simple pattern: a Bible verse, a statement of faith, then a sentence that says, in effect, we reject the false teaching. The first article opens with the words of Jesus in John. In the King James Bible: "I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me." Then the line today's carry is drawn from: Jesus Christ, as the Bible bears witness to him, is the one Word of God that the church must hear, trust and obey, in life and in death. And the rejection: the church may not treat any other event, power, figure or truth as God's revelation alongside him. Read that in a country where some church voices were hailing the leader as a gift from God, and you hear it without a single name. John's Gospel opens, "In the beginning was the Word," and calls Jesus that Word. Barmen leans on it: one Word, not one Word plus a nation, a race or a leader. Now the honest part. Barmen defended the church's freedom to preach Christ. It said nothing directly about the Jews being driven from their jobs and homes, and later Christians, including some who were there, came to see that silence as a failure. Barmen is still read in churches, often by Lutheran and Reformed Christians, as a model of saying no, and as a reminder of what that no left out.
screen: `TO CONFESS: TO SAY IT OUT LOUD.`

segments.voice: Lord here just means whatever gets the final say. Ask what decides things in your life when it's hard: money, fear, a boss, a belief; notice it without judging, then ask what you'd want to have the final say. If you pray, say quietly: I am the way, the truth, and the life; if not, name the one thing you won't hand over to anyone.
Barmen. The German town where the Confessing Church declared that Jesus Christ alone, and no state or leader, is the Word the church must obey.
Your line: Jesus Christ is the one Word. One Word, not one Word plus. Day nine hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Some Lutheran, Reformed and united Protestant churches include the Barmen Declaration among their confessional documents, and it is read and studied in congregations, especially when churches discuss faith and political power.

chat.who: a friend in your history class
chat.says: The Barmen Declaration never even names Hitler. So how was it a protest?
options: It said Jesus Christ alone is the Word the church obeys, so no leader could share that place.
It wasn't really a protest; it only settled an argument about how services should be run.
It praised the new state, but politely asked that pastors keep being paid by the church.
chat.meaning: Barmen's first article calls Jesus Christ the one Word of God and rejects any other power, figure or truth beside him: no name needed.

German Christians.meaning: the pro-Nazi church movement that Barmen opposed

Confessing Church.meaning: the Protestants who said out loud what they believed, at Barmen

Karl Barth.meaning: the Swiss theologian who did much of the drafting

Lutherans.meaning: Protestants in the tradition of Martin Luther

Reformed.meaning: Protestants in the tradition of John Calvin

notes: Claims rule: no date, no count of delegates or churches. 'Some pastors go along. Others don't.' is a general claim; soften if needed.

Article 1 is paraphrased, not quoted (English translations of the declaration may be under copyright). Confirm the paraphrase: 'one Word of God which we have to hear, and which we have to trust and obey in life and in death', and the rejection of 'other events and powers, figures and truths'.
Article 1 also cites John 10:1, 9; only John 14:6 is quoted here.
The German Christians' aims (a Reich bishop, the 'Aryan paragraph' excluding pastors of Jewish descent): confirm phrasing.
Barth's role in drafting: 'did much of the drafting'; confirm.
The critique that Barmen was silent on the persecution of Jews is widely made, including by participants later; confirm the phrase 'including some who signed'.
Barmen's confessional status varies by church; confirm the howItsDone wording.
